## Question Four: If Puma want to target elite runners, where should they focus their efforts?
```{r prepare-data-for-elite-classification, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="center", message=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# Clean and prepare the data - using grade for elite classification
clean_data <- parkrun_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(Time_seconds) & Time_seconds > 0 & !is.na(grade)) %>%
  mutate(
    Time_minutes = Time_seconds / 60,
    elite_runner = grade >= 70,  
    week = as.factor(week),
    Gender = factor(Gender, levels = c("M", "F"))  # Ensure consistent gender coding
  )
```

In order to target elite runner for the marketing campaign, we can look at the "Age grade" of each runners. "Age grade" is a percentage that compares runner's time to the world record for runner's age and gender. 

This percentage could be understood as:
- <50% = beginner 
- 50-60% = average 
- 60-70% = good 
- 70-80% = very good 
- 80%+ = excellent

A person who has an age grade above 70 would be consider as an elite runner, this applies to both men and women.  Here is the table shows the number of elite runners between parkruns.


```{r}
# Overall elite analysis by location
elite_analysis_overall <- clean_data %>%
  group_by(parkrun) %>%
  summarise(
    total_runners = n(),
    elite_runners = sum(elite_runner),
    elite_percentage = elite_runners / total_runners * 100,
    avg_grade = mean(grade, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(elite_runners))%>% 
  rename(
    "Parkrun Location" = parkrun,
    "Total Runners" = total_runners,
    "Elite runners" = elite_runners,
    "Elite runners percentage" =  elite_percentage,
    "Average grade" = avg_grade
  )

elite_analysis_overall %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Table 4.1. Overal Elite Analysis by Parkrun Location",
    digits = 2
  )
```
It's noticeable to find that the Hagley parkrun has an outstanding numbers of elite runner but Scarborough parkrun has the highest elite runner percentage and highest average grade among these parkruns. 


```{r elite-runner-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# Analyze elite runners by location and gender
elite_analysis_gender <- clean_data %>%
  group_by(parkrun, Gender) %>%
  summarise(
    total_runners = n(),
    elite_runners = sum(elite_runner),
    elite_percentage = elite_runners / total_runners * 100,
    avg_grade = mean(grade, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_grade = max(grade, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(parkrun) %>% 
  rename(
    "Parkrun Location" = parkrun,
    "Total Runners" = total_runners,
    "Elite runners" = elite_runners,
    "Elite runners percentage" =  elite_percentage,
    "Average grade" = avg_grade,
    "Max grade" = max_grade
  )

elite_analysis_gender %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Table 4.2 Elite Analysis by Gender and Parkrun Location",
    digits = 2
  )
```
Here is a bar chart to demonstrate the difference number of elite runners by location and gender. The number of men elite runners tend to double than the number of women elite runner in every parkruns. Hagley parkrun has the most both men and women elite runner, second is Scarborough, third is Peagsus.
```{r elite-runner-visualisaion, echo=FALSE}

# Bar chart: Number of elite runners by location and gender
p1 <- ggplot(elite_analysis_gender, aes(x = reorder(`Parkrun Location`, -`Elite runners`), y = `Elite runners`, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = `Elite runners`), 
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), 
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("M" = "steelblue", "F" = "pink"),
                    labels = c("M" = "Male", "F" = "Female")) +
  labs(title = "Number of Elite Runners by Location and Gender",
       subtitle = "Elite runners defined as Grade >= 70%",
       x = "Location", 
       y = "Number of Elite Runners",
       fill = "Gender") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "top")

p1

```
But if we look at the percentage distribution, Scarborough has the most percentage of men elite runner then Hagley and Pegasus. And the most percentage of women elite runner belongs to Hagley.  
```{r percentage-elite-runner-visualisation, echo=FALSE}
# Bar chart: Percentage of elite runners by location and gender
p2 <- ggplot(elite_analysis_gender, aes(x = reorder(`Parkrun Location`, -`Elite runners percentage`), y = `Elite runners percentage`, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(`Elite runners percentage`, 1), "%")), 
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), 
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("M" = "steelblue", "F" = "pink"),
                    labels = c("M" = "Male", "F" = "Female")) +
  labs(title = "Percentage of Elite Runners by Location and Gender",
       subtitle = "Elite runners defined as Grade >= 70%",
       x = "Location", 
       y = "Percentage of Elite Runners (%)",
       fill = "Gender") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "top")
p2
```
To make Puma campaign targeting elite runners effective, Hagley parkrun is the most suitable place. Second place would be Scarborough then Pegasus.

## Question Five: What locations feature the most consistent runners?
```{r collect-consistent-runner, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.alt= "center"}
# Puma believe more consistent runners have better potential as customers, how many runners are consistent and is consistency different across locations?

# Identify consistent runners (appearing in multiple weeks)
runner_consistency <- clean_data %>%
  group_by(name_id, parkrun) %>%
  summarise(
    weeks_participated = n_distinct(week),
    total_runs = n(),
    avg_time = mean(Time_minutes),
    first_week = min(as.numeric(as.character(week))),
    last_week = max(as.numeric(as.character(week)))
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    consistency_level = case_when(
      weeks_participated >= 5 ~ "Highly Consistent (5+ weeks)",
      weeks_participated >= 3 ~ "Moderately Consistent (3-4 weeks)",
      TRUE ~ "Occasional (1-2 weeks)"
    )
  )

runner_consistency
```
Another potential customers group is the consistent runners. The table shows the number of consistent runners group by location. Consistent runners would be recognized if they had attended from 3 to 4 weeks, we would consider highly consistent runners if they had attend from more than 5 weeks. And a runner joined 1 or 2 weeks would be considered as occasionally. 

```{r consistent-runner-table, echo=FALSE, include= TRUE}
# Consistency summary by location
consistency_by_location <- runner_consistency %>%
  group_by(parkrun) %>%
  summarise(
    total_unique_runners = n(),
    highly_consistent = sum(weeks_participated >= 5),
    moderately_consistent = sum(weeks_participated >= 3 & weeks_participated <= 4),
    occasional = sum(weeks_participated <= 2),
    pct_highly_consistent = highly_consistent / total_unique_runners * 100,
    avg_weeks_per_runner = mean(weeks_participated)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_weeks_per_runner)) %>% 
   rename(
    "Parkrun Location" = parkrun,
    "Total Unique Runners" = total_unique_runners,
    "Highly Consistent (5+ Weeks)" = highly_consistent,
    "Moderately Consistent (3–4 Weeks)" = moderately_consistent,
    "Occasional (1–2 Weeks)" = occasional,
    "Percentage Highly Consistent (%)" = pct_highly_consistent,
    "Average Weeks per Runner" = avg_weeks_per_runner
  )

consistency_by_location %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Table 4.1 Number of consistent runner in each parkrun ",
    digits = 2
  )

```
There is no doubt that Hagley parkrun has the most number of highly and moderately consistent runners. Foster and Pegasus parkrun has the second and third of number of highly consistent runners consecutively. Scarborough only place the fourth in highly consistent runners but it has the second most of the moderately consistent runner. Also the number of moderately consistent runners in Riverlution parkun is quiet noticeable because the dataset for Riverlution is just 8 weeks in stead of 11 weeks like other parkrun but it has almost equal amount as Scarborough and Foster.

In the number aspect, Hagley has the most number of consitent runners but when it come to percentage, Pegasus parkrun has the most percentage of highly consistent runners. At the second and third place are Foster and Hagley consecutively.

```{r, echo=FALSE, include= TRUE}
# Consistency level breakdown
p4 <- runner_consistency %>%
  count(parkrun, consistency_level) %>%
  group_by(parkrun) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = parkrun, y = percentage, fill = consistency_level)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Highly Consistent (5+ weeks)" = "#2E8B57", 
                               "Moderately Consistent (3-4 weeks)" = "#FFA500", 
                               "Occasional (1-2 weeks)" = "#CD5C5C")) +
  labs(title = "Runner Consistency Distribution by Location",
       subtitle = "Breakdown of runner participation patterns",
       x = "Location", y = "Percentage (%)", fill = "Consistency Level") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")

p4
```
And if we compare the average weeks participation among location, it has the same order of top 3.

```{r consistency-visualisation, echo=FALSE, include= TRUE }
# Visualize consistency patterns
# Consistency distribution by location
p3 <- ggplot(consistency_by_location, 
             aes(x = reorder(`Parkrun Location`, -`Average Weeks per Runner`), 
                 y = `Average Weeks per Runner`)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(`Average Weeks per Runner`, 1)), 
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Weeks Participation by Location",
    subtitle = "Higher values indicate a more consistent runner base",
    x = "Location",
    y = "Average Weeks per Runner"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

print(p3)
```
If Puma want to reach out the most number of consistent runners, Hagley will be the best option. Although, the percentage of the consistent runners and the average weeks participated of each runner in Pegasus and Foster are high, the number of highly consistent runners are just a half of Hagley. On the other hand, the number of consistent runners in Riverlution is promising if Puma want to focus on consistent runners as the potential customer.
